Work done equals the **change in kinetic energy**, and kinetic energy goes as the
**square** of the speed.
**Step 1 — find the work from rest to v.**
W₁ = ½mv² − 0
= **½mv²** ✓
**Step 2 — find the work from v to 2v.**
W₂ = ½m(2v)² − ½mv²
= ½m(4v²) − ½mv²
= 2mv² − ½mv²
= **(3/2)mv²** ✓
**Step 3 — take the ratio.**
W₂/W₁ = (3/2)mv²/(½mv²)
= **3** ✓
**Step 4 — conclude.** Accelerating from v to 2v takes **three times** the work needed to
reach v from rest ✓
**Why the second stage costs so much more.** Energy goes as **v²**, so the increments
are not equal ✓ Going from 0 to v buys one unit of energy; going from v to 2v buys
three more, since 4 − 1 = 3.
**The pattern in successive stages.**
0 → v: **1** unit
v → 2v: **3** units ✓
2v → 3v: **5** units
3v → 4v: **7** units
the **odd numbers** again - the same 1 : 3 : 5 : 7 pattern that governs distances in
successive equal time intervals from rest.
**A worked instance.** A 1000 kg truck with v = 10 m s⁻¹:
0 → 10 m s⁻¹: ½(1000)(100) = **50 kJ**
10 → 20 m s⁻¹: ½(1000)(400 − 100) = **150 kJ** ✓ exactly three times.
**The practical consequence.** Overtaking at speed demands far more energy - and fuel -
than starting from rest ✓ It is also why high-speed collisions are so much more
destructive: all that energy must go somewhere in the crash.
**Why the time or distance taken is irrelevant.** The work-energy theorem depends only
on the **endpoints** ✓ Whether the truck accelerates gently over a kilometre or sharply
over a hundred metres, the work is the same.
**Reading the distractors.** "**Four times**" ✗ confuses the ratio of **energies**, 4 : 1,
with the ratio of the **work increments**, 3 : 1 - the commonest error here. "**Same**"
✗ assumes energy is linear in v, and "**less**" ✗ reverses the trend ✓
∴ three times as the work done in accelerating it from rest to v.

Alpha decay conserves **momentum**: the nucleus was at rest, so the fragments carry equal
and opposite momenta.
**Step 1 — identify the two fragments.** The parent ᴬ_ZX emits an alpha particle of mass
number **4**, leaving a daughter of mass number **A − 4** ✓
**Step 2 — conserve momentum.** The parent is at rest, so the total momentum stays
zero:
0 = 4v + (A − 4)V ✓
taking mass numbers as proportional to the masses.
**Step 3 — solve for the recoil speed.**
(A − 4)V = −4v
**|V| = 4v/(A − 4)** ✓
the minus sign showing the daughter recoils in the **opposite** direction.
**Why mass numbers may be used in place of masses.** Both masses are multiples of
roughly the same atomic mass unit, and the constant cancels in the ratio ✓ The small
mass defect is negligible at this level of accuracy.
**A worked instance - the decay of uranium-238.**
A = 238, so A − 4 = **234**
V = 4v/234 = **v/58·5** ✓
With the alpha leaving at about 1·4 x 10⁷ m s⁻¹, the daughter thorium nucleus recoils at
only **2·4 x 10⁵ m s⁻¹** - fast by everyday standards, but a small fraction of the
alpha's speed.
**How the energy is shared.** With equal momenta, E = p²/2m, so the energies go
**inversely** as the masses ✓
E_alpha/E_daughter = (A − 4)/4
For uranium that is **58·5 : 1** - the alpha carries about 98% of the released energy,
which is why alpha particles are so penetrating while the recoil nucleus stops almost at
once.
**Why the recoil matters in practice.** The recoiling nucleus deposits its energy within
a few atomic spacings, doing intense local damage ✓ This is the basis of the "hot
particle" hazard from inhaled alpha emitters.
**A check on the limit.** For very heavy parents, A − 4 ≫ 4, so V ≪ v ✓ as the formula
requires - the heavy daughter barely moves.
**Reading the distractors.** **(A − 4)/4v** ✗ is the **reciprocal** and has the wrong
dimensions. **v** ✗ would need equal masses, and **v/4** ✗ divides by the alpha's mass
number rather than the daughter's ✓
∴ 4v/(A − 4).

When **equal distances** are covered at different speeds, the average speed is the
**harmonic mean**.
**Step 1 — state the definition.**
average speed = **total distance/total time** ✓ not the arithmetic mean of the speeds.
**Step 2 — let each leg be d.**
time out: t₁ = d/30
time back: t₂ = d/20 ✓
**Step 3 — form the average.**
v_av = 2d/(d/30 + d/20)
= 2/(1/30 + 1/20) ✓
**Step 4 — evaluate.**
1/30 + 1/20 = (2 + 3)/60 = **5/60 = 1/12**
v_av = 2/(1/12)
= **24 km h⁻¹** ✓
**The formula to remember.** For two equal distances,
**v_av = 2v₁v₂/(v₁ + v₂)** ✓
= 2(30)(20)/50 = 1200/50 = **24 km h⁻¹** ✓ in one line.
**Why the answer is below 25.** The car spends **more time** at the slower speed, so the
slow leg is weighted more heavily ✓ The harmonic mean always lies **below** the
arithmetic mean, and the gap grows as the two speeds diverge.
**A check with a concrete distance.** Take d = 60 km:
out: 60/30 = **2 h**
back: 60/20 = **3 h**
total: 120 km in **5 h** = **24 km h⁻¹** ✓
**When the arithmetic mean would be right.** If the car spent **equal times** at the two
speeds rather than covering equal distances ✓ Then the average would be (30 + 20)/2 =
25 km h⁻¹ - which is exactly the first distractor.
**The two cases, side by side.**
equal **distances** → **harmonic** mean, 2v₁v₂/(v₁ + v₂) ✓
equal **times** → **arithmetic** mean, (v₁ + v₂)/2 ✓
Deciding which applies is the whole of this question.
**What the average velocity would be.** The car returns to its starting point, so the
**displacement is zero** and the average **velocity** is **0** ✓ - a different quantity
entirely from the average speed.
**Reading the distractors.** **25 km h⁻¹** ✗ is the arithmetic mean. **50 km h⁻¹** ✗
adds the speeds, and **10 km h⁻¹** ✗ subtracts them ✓
∴ 24 kmph.

From rest with constant acceleration, distance goes as **t²**, so compute both halves
and compare.
**Step 1 — find the distance in the first half of the time.**
x₁ = ½a(t/2)²
= ½a(t²/4)
= **at²/8** ✓
**Step 2 — find the total distance in time t.**
x_total = ½at²
= **4at²/8** ✓
**Step 3 — subtract to get the second half.**
x₂ = 4at²/8 − at²/8
= **3at²/8** ✓
**Step 4 — compare.**
x₂/x₁ = 3
**x₂ = 3x₁** ✓
**Why the second half covers three times as much.** The body is **faster** throughout
it ✓ Its average speed over the first half is at/4, and over the second half 3at/4 -
exactly three times - so with equal durations the distances are in the ratio 1 : 3.
**The underlying rule.** In successive equal time intervals from rest, the distances go
as **1 : 3 : 5 : 7 …** ✓ the odd numbers, because the cumulative distances go as
1 : 4 : 9 : 16 and the differences of squares are the odd numbers.
**A worked check.** Take a = 2 m s⁻² and t = 4 s:
first 2 s: x₁ = ½(2)(4) = **4 m**
whole 4 s: ½(2)(16) = **16 m**
second 2 s: 16 − 4 = **12 m** ✓ three times x₁.
**The speeds at each stage.**
at t/2: v = at/2
at t: v = at ✓
The velocity doubles over the second half while the distance triples - because distance
depends on the **average** speed over the interval, not the final one.
**Why "starts from rest" matters.** With a non-zero initial velocity the ratio would be
different ✓ For example, at constant velocity the two halves would be **equal**, and
the whole pattern of odd numbers depends on starting from rest.
**Reading the distractors.** **x₂ = x₁** ✗ describes uniform velocity. **x₂ = 2x₁** ✗
and **x₂ = 4x₁** ✗ match no stage of the motion ✓ Working out both halves explicitly, as
above, settles it in two lines.
∴ x₂ = 3x₁.

In **free fall** everything accelerates together, so the spring balance registers
nothing.
**Step 1 — write Newton's second law for the mass.** With the lift falling freely, the
mass accelerates downward at **g**:
mg − T = ma = mg ✓
**Step 2 — solve for the tension.**
T = mg − mg
= **0** ✓
**Step 3 — read the balance.** A spring balance measures the **tension in its spring**,
which is zero, so the reading is **zero** ✓
**Why this is weightlessness.** The mass and the balance are both falling at the same
rate, so the spring is neither stretched nor compressed ✓ The body is in **free fall**,
and its **apparent weight** is zero - though its **actual weight** mg is unchanged, and
gravity is acting on it as strongly as ever.
**The general formula.** For a lift accelerating with a (upward positive),
apparent weight = **m(g + a)** ✓
at rest or constant velocity, a = 0: reading **mg**, that is **50 kg** ✓
accelerating **up**: reading **more** than 50 kg
accelerating **down**: reading **less** than 50 kg
**free fall**, a = −g: reading **zero** ✓
**Where this is experienced.** Astronauts in orbit are in exactly this state ✓ The space
station and everything in it fall together around the Earth, so nothing presses on
anything else. They are **not** beyond gravity - at 400 km, g is still about 89% of its
surface value.
**The "vomit comet".** Aircraft flying parabolic arcs reproduce free fall for 20 to 30
seconds at a time ✓ used for training and for microgravity experiments.
**What the balance really measures.** Never the weight directly, but the **force the
spring must exert** to support the mass ✓ In free fall no support is needed, so the
force - and the reading - is zero.
**Reading the distractors.** **= 50 kg** ✗ is the reading at rest or in uniform motion.
**> 50 kg** ✗ would need upward acceleration, and **< 50 kg** but non-zero ✗ would need
a downward acceleration **less** than g - a lift braking, or descending on a cable ✓
Free fall is the extreme case.
∴ = 0.

Only the **vertical** component of the Earth's field threads the horizontal area the
wings sweep.
**Step 1 — find the vertical component.** With a dip angle δ, the total field B divides
as
B_v = B sin δ ✓
= (4 x 10⁻⁴) sin 30°
= (4 x 10⁻⁴)(0·5)
= **2 x 10⁻⁴ T** ✓
**Step 2 — apply the motional emf formula.**
e = B_v l v
= (2 x 10⁻⁴)(20)(400) ✓
**Step 3 — evaluate.**
2 x 10⁻⁴ x 20 = **4 x 10⁻³**
4 x 10⁻³ x 400 = **1·6 V** ✓
**Why only the vertical component counts.** The aircraft flies horizontally and the
wingspan is horizontal, so the area swept out per second is **horizontal** ✓ Only a
field component **perpendicular** to that area - the vertical one - contributes flux.
**What the dip angle means.** The angle the Earth's **total** field makes with the
horizontal ✓ It is 0° at the magnetic equator and 90° at the magnetic poles; 30° places
this aircraft at low latitudes.
**The three field quantities.**
B_H = B cos δ = 4 x 10⁻⁴ x 0·866 = **3·46 x 10⁻⁴ T**
B_v = B sin δ = **2 x 10⁻⁴ T** ✓
and tan δ = B_v/B_H, the usual relation.
**Where the emf comes from.** Each free electron in the wing moves with the aircraft and
feels a force qv̄ x B̄ **along** the wingspan ✓ Charge piles up at one tip until its
electrostatic field balances the magnetic force, and the resulting potential difference
is the emf.
**Can it be used?** No ✓ There is no circuit - the air does not conduct - so no current
flows and no energy is extracted. The voltage is real but idle.
**Why the direction of flight matters only for the sign.** Flying west rather than east
reverses which wingtip is positive, but the magnitude is unchanged ✓
**Reading the distractors.** **3·2 V** ✗ uses the **total** field instead of its
vertical component. **0·8 V** ✗ halves it again, and **6·4 V** ✗ doubles 3·2 ✓ The
factor sin 30° = ½ is the step the question is testing.
∴ 1.6 V.

A moderator's job is to **slow the neutrons down** so that they can cause further
fission.
**Step 1 — see the problem it solves.** Neutrons released in fission are **fast**,
carrying about **2 MeV** ✓ But uranium-235 is far more likely to capture a **slow**
(thermal) neutron - its fission cross-section at 0·025 eV is hundreds of times larger
than at 2 MeV.
**Step 2 — see how the moderator works.** Fast neutrons collide **elastically** with the
moderator's light nuclei, losing energy at each bounce ✓ After enough collisions they
reach **thermal** energies, about 0·025 eV, and the chain reaction can be sustained.
**Step 3 — conclude.** The moderator decreases the **speed of the neutrons** ✓
**Why light nuclei are needed.** In an elastic collision, the energy transferred is
greatest when the two masses are **equal** ✓ A neutron striking a proton can lose
almost all its energy in a single hit; striking a heavy nucleus it merely bounces off
with little loss - which is why lead makes a useless moderator.
**The common moderators.**
**ordinary water** - cheap and very effective per collision, but it absorbs some
neutrons, so enriched fuel is needed ✓
**heavy water (D₂O)** - absorbs far less, allowing natural uranium to be used; the basis
of the CANDU and of India's PHWR reactors ✓
**graphite** - used in the first reactor, Fermi's pile of 1942
**Why not simply reduce the number of neutrons.** That is the **control rod's** job ✓
Cadmium or boron rods **absorb** neutrons and are moved in or out to hold the chain
reaction exactly critical. The moderator does not absorb; it slows.
**The three components, distinguished.**
**moderator**: slows the neutrons ✓
**control rods**: absorb them, regulating the rate ✓
**coolant**: removes the heat produced
In a pressurised water reactor, water serves as both moderator and coolant - a useful
safety feature, since losing the water also stops the reaction.
**Reading the distractors.** "**Number of neutrons**" ✗ describes the control rods.
"**Escape of neutrons**" ✗ describes the **reflector**. "**Temperature of the
reactor**" ✗ describes the coolant ✓
∴ speed of neutrons.

Equal **distances** at different speeds give the **harmonic mean**, not the arithmetic
one.
**Step 1 — let each half be d.**
t₁ = d/40
t₂ = d/50 ✓
**Step 2 — form the average speed.**
v_av = total distance/total time
= 2d/(d/40 + d/50) ✓
**Step 3 — evaluate the bracket.**
1/40 + 1/50 = (5 + 4)/200 = **9/200**
**Step 4 — divide.**
v_av = 2/(9/200)
= 400/9
= **44·44 km h⁻¹** ✓
**The compact formula.**
v_av = **2v₁v₂/(v₁ + v₂)** ✓
= 2(40)(50)/90 = 4000/90 = **44·44 km h⁻¹** ✓
**Why the answer is below 45.** The car spends **longer** on the slower half, so the
40 km/h leg carries more weight ✓ The harmonic mean always lies below the arithmetic
mean (45 here), and the two coincide only when the speeds are equal.
**A check with a concrete distance.** Take the total journey as 400 km, so each half is
200 km:
first half: 200/40 = **5 h**
second half: 200/50 = **4 h**
total: 400 km in **9 h** = **44·44 km h⁻¹** ✓
**When to use which mean.**
equal **distances** → harmonic mean ✓
equal **times** → arithmetic mean, here (40 + 50)/2 = **45 km h⁻¹** ✓ which is the first
distractor, and the trap.
**How far apart the two means can be.** For speeds of 10 and 90, the arithmetic mean is
50 but the harmonic mean is only **18** ✓ The more unequal the speeds, the more the slow
leg dominates - which is why a short stretch of heavy traffic ruins a journey time.
**Why average speed is never a simple average.** It is defined as **total distance over
total time**, and only that definition is safe ✓ Any shortcut must be checked against
it.
**Reading the distractors.** **45·00** ✗ is the arithmetic mean. **43·14** ✗ and
**42·04** ✗ match no standard combination of 40 and 50 ✓
∴ 44.44 km/h.
